facts.statement: The genus Anchiornis was described by Xu et al. in 2009.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Xu et al., 2009

facts.statement: Anchiornis fossils date to the Late Jurassic (Oxfordian) period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Jurassic (Oxfordian),

facts.statement: Anchiornis fossils have been found exclusively in the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning, China.
facts.quote: Anchiornis fossils have been found only in the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning, China

facts.statement: Anchiornis lived about 160 million years ago during the Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: in rocks dated to the Late Jurassic, about 160 million years ago

facts.statement: The type specimen of Anchiornis was found in the Yaolugou area of Jianchang County, Liaoning, China.
facts.quote: The first known fossil of Anchiornis (its type specimen) was dug up in the Yaolugou area of Jianchang County, Liaoning, China

facts.statement: Most studies date the rocks containing Anchiornis to 160.89 to 160.25 million years ago.
facts.quote: These rocks have been difficult to date, but most studies have concluded that they belong to the Tiaojishan Formation of rocks dated to the late Jurassic period (Oxfordian age), 160.89 to 160.25 million years old

facts.statement: Anchiornis was described by Xu Xing and colleagues in 2009.
facts.quote: Anchiornis was studied and described by paleontologist Xu Xing and colleagues in a paper accepted to the Chinese Science Bulletin in 2009

facts.statement: The type specimen of Anchiornis is held at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology with catalogue number IVPP V14378.
facts.quote: The specimen is currently in the collection of the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology with the catalogue number IVPP V14378

facts.statement: The species name huxleyi honors Thomas Henry Huxley.
facts.quote: The name Anchiornis huxleyi was chosen by Xu and colleagues in honor of Thomas Henry Huxley

facts.statement: A second Anchiornis specimen found around the same time is catalogued as LPM – B00 169 in the Liaoning Paleontological Museum.
facts.quote: It was assigned the catalogue number LPM – B00 169 in the Liaoning Paleontological Museum

facts.statement: A nearly complete Anchiornis skeleton missing the tail was reported in 2010.
facts.quote: One of these, a nearly complete skeleton missing the tail, also preserving extensive feather remains, was reported in 2010

facts.statement: The Shandong Tianyu Museum of Nature reported holding 255 Anchiornis specimens in 2010.
facts.quote: The Shandong Tianyu Museum of Nature in Pingyi County, China, for example, was reported to hold 255 specimens of Anchiornis in its collections in 2010

facts.statement: There is only one known species of Anchiornis, Anchiornis huxleyi.
facts.quote: with only one known species, the type species Anchiornis huxleyi

facts.statement: Anchiornis huxleyi was a small, bipedal theropod with a triangular skull sharing features with dromaeosaurids, troodontids, and primitive avialans.
facts.quote: Anchiornis huxleyi was a small, bipedal theropod dinosaur with a triangular skull bearing several details in common with dromaeosaurids, troodontids, and primitive avialans

facts.statement: Anchiornis was about the size of a crow.
facts.quote: Like other early paravians, Anchiornis was small, about the size of a crow

facts.statement: Anchiornis was covered in feathers but also had scales on certain body parts.
facts.quote: Like all paravians, it was covered in feathers, though it also had scales on certain parts of the body

facts.statement: The holotype of Anchiornis measured 34 cm in length and weighed 110 grams.
facts.quote: The holotype, belonging to a subadult or young adult individual, measured 34 cm long and weighed 110 g

facts.statement: The largest Anchiornis specimens measured 60 to 62 cm in length, had a wingspan of nearly 57.4 cm, and weighed between 0.6 and 1 kg.
facts.quote: The largest specimens measured 60 - 62 cm in total body length, nearly 57.4 cm in wingspan and weighed about 0.6 - 1 kg

facts.statement: The status of Aurornis xui, Eosinopteryx brevipenna, and Serikornis sungei as synonyms of Anchiornis is questioned.
facts.quote: synonyms: * Aurornis xui? Godefroit et al., 2013 Eosinopteryx brevipenna? Godefroit et al., 2013 Serikornis sungei? Lefèvre et al., 2017

facts.statement: The wings of Anchiornis contained approximately 20 to 28 primary feathers, with significant variation observed between individuals.
facts.quote: The wing of Anchiornis was composed of around 20-28 primary feathers, with research showing much variation among individuals.

facts.statement: Anchiornis wing feathers had curved, symmetrical quills with rounded tips, suggesting poor aerodynamic capability.
facts.quote: The wing feathers had curved but symmetrical central quills, with small and thin relative size, and rounded tips, all indicating poor aerodynamic ability.

facts.statement: In Anchiornis, the longest wing feathers were located near the wrist, creating a broad, rounded profile that was less adapted for flight compared to Microraptor or Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: However, in Anchiornis, the longest wing feathers were those nearest the wrist, making the wing broadest in the middle and tapering near the tip for a more rounded, less flight-adapted profile.

facts.statement: Anchiornis had a propatagium covered in covert feathers that smoothed the wing and filled gaps between primary and secondary feathers.
facts.quote: In Anchiornis, this part of the wing was covered in covert feathers which smoothed the wing and covered the gaps between the larger primary and secondary feathers.

facts.statement: Some Anchiornis fossils show multiple layers of covert feathers covering most of the wing surface, strengthening the wing structure.
facts.quote: In some Anchiornis fossils, on the other hand, several layers of covert feathers seem to extend down to cover most of the wing's surface, so that the wing is essentially made of multiple layers of feathers, rather than a layer of broad feathers with only their bases hidden by layers of coverts.

facts.statement: Anchiornis had three clawed fingers on its wing, but the two longest were bound together by skin and tissue, making it functionally two-fingered.
facts.quote: The wing included three clawed fingers; however, unlike in some more primitive theropods, the longest two fingers were not separate, but were bound together by the skin and other tissue forming the wing, so Anchiornis was functionally two-fingered.

facts.statement: Anchiornis had long, vaned feathers on its hind legs, leading some scientists to classify it as a four-winged dinosaur.
facts.quote: In addition to the front wings, Anchiornis had long, vaned feathers on the hind legs. This has led many scientists to call Anchiornis a four-winged dinosaur, along with similar animals like Microraptor and Sapeornis.

facts.statement: The hind leg feathers of Anchiornis likely served a display function rather than flight, as they lacked the shape and arrangement of true flight feathers.
facts.quote: However, the feathers on the hind legs in Anchiornis did not have the shape or arrangement expected from flight feathers, and it is likely that their primary role was in display rather than flight.

facts.statement: Although Anchiornis had long legs typically associated with strong running, its extensive leg feathers suggest this trait may be vestigial.
facts.quote: Anchiornis had very long legs, which is usually an indication that an animal is a strong runner. However, the extensive leg feathers indicate that this may be a vestigial trait, as running animals tend to have reduced, not increased, hair or feathers on their legs.

facts.statement: Anchiornis had four toes on its foot, with the third and fourth being the longest.
facts.quote: Like most paravians, Anchiornis had four toes on the foot, with the third and fourth toes the longest.

facts.statement: The hallux (first toe) of Anchiornis was not reversed, unlike in perching bird species.
facts.quote: The first toe, or hallux, was not reversed as in perching species.

facts.statement: Anchiornis hindwings were shorter than those of Microraptor, consisting of 12 to 13 feathers on the tibia and 10 to 11 on the tarsus.
facts.quote: The hindwings of Anchiornis were also shorter than those of Microraptor, and were made up of 12 to 13 flight feathers anchored to the tibia (lower leg) and 10 to 11 to the tarsus (upper foot).

facts.statement: Unlike Microraptor, Anchiornis hindwing feathers were longest near the body, with foot feathers short and directed downward perpendicular to the foot bones.
facts.quote: Unlike Microraptor, the hindwing feathers were longest closer to the body, with the foot feathers being short and directed downward, almost perpendicular to the foot bones.

facts.statement: Preserved scales on the toes, tarsus, and tibia of some Anchiornis specimens suggest that scales existed beneath the feathers.
facts.quote: Some specimens have preserved scales on the toes, tarsus, and even lower leg (tibia), suggesting that scales existed beneath the feathers.

facts.statement: In 2010, scientists examined a well-preserved Anchiornis specimen at the Beijing Museum of Natural History to map its coloration using melanosomes.
facts.quote: In 2010, a team of scientists examined numerous points among the feathers of an extremely well-preserved Anchiornis specimen in the Beijing Museum of Natural History to survey the distribution of melanosomes, the pigment cells that give feathers their color.

facts.statement: A 2015 study of a second Anchiornis fossil found only gray-black melanosomes, contradicting the 2010 findings of rufous coloration.
facts.quote: In 2015, a second Anchiornis fossil at the Yizhou Fossil & Geology Park was subjected to a similar study that included a survey of melanosome shapes across all the feathers. In contrast to the 2010 study, only gray-black type melanosomes were found.

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesized that the rufous color might have been replaced as the smaller Beijing Museum specimen aged.
facts.quote: Second, because the Beijing Museum specimen was smaller, it is possible that the rufous color was replaced as these animals aged.

facts.statement: It is debated whether regional differences or distinct species of Anchiornis caused the variation in plumage color patterns.
facts.quote: Third, it is possible that there were regional differences or even different species of Anchiornis which had different color patterns in their plumage.

facts.statement: Avialans are more closely related to modern birds than to dromaeosaurid and troodontid dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Members of Avialae, called avialans, are all more closely related to modern birds than they are to dromaeosaurid and troodontid dinosaurs

facts.statement: Hu Dongyu and colleagues reclassified Anchiornis as a troodontid based on features in the second specimen.
facts.quote: Hu Dongyu and his colleagues to reclassify Anchiornis as a troodontid

facts.statement: One study classified Anchiornis as a member of Archaeopterygidae, placing it as more primitive than dromaeosaurids, troodontids, or avialans.
facts.quote: One study found Anchiornis to be a member of Archaeopterygidae

facts.statement: Studies have debated whether Anchiornis was an avialan, with later findings concluding it was likely a basal member of Paraves outside the clade containing dromaeosaurids, troodontids, and avialans.
facts.quote: More comprehensive studies suggested that Anchiornis may have been an avialan after all, though new finds and updated versions of the same study later reversed this finding

facts.statement: A 2017 re-evaluation placed Anchiornis in the family Anchiornithidae alongside genera like Eosinopteryx and Xiaotingia.
facts.quote: In a 2017 re-evaluation of the Haarlem Archaeopteryx specimen, Anchiornis was found to be in a group with other genera, like Eosinopteryx, Xiaotingia, and was placed in the family Anchiornithidae

facts.statement: Anchiornis displayed complex coloration with speckled patterns across its body and wings, likely used for communication or display.
facts.quote: Anchiornis exhibited a complex pattern of coloration with different colors in speckled patterns across the body and wings

facts.statement: Anchiornis had forelimbs measuring 80% of the total length of its hindlimbs.
facts.quote: Anchiornis is notable for its proportionally long forelimbs, which measured 80% of the total length of the hindlimbs

facts.statement: Researchers initially speculated that Anchiornis could fly or glide, but later studies suggested it was likely flightless due to heavy body weight relative to wing area.
facts.quote: The authors initially speculated that it would have been possible for Anchiornis to fly or glide

facts.statement: A 2016 study suggested juvenile Anchiornis might have used wings to assist running up inclines, though adults likely could not gain aerodynamic benefits from flapping.
facts.quote: A 2016 study of potential flight performance in early paravians concluded that while juvenile Anchiornis specimens may have been able to use their wings to assist running up an incline

facts.statement: Anchiornis likely lacked a bony breastbone (sternum), possibly having one made of cartilage instead.
facts.quote: Notably, Anchiornis seems to have lacked a breastbone (sternum), which may have been made of cartilage rather than bone

facts.statement: A 2025 study of nine specimens with 20-28 primary feathers suggested Anchiornis performed irregular moulting, indicating it was probably flightless.
facts.quote: In 2025, Kiat and colleagues examined nine specimens which preserved 20-28 primary feathers and three series of primary covert feathers

facts.statement: Anchiornis had hindleg proportions similar to primitive theropods, suggesting a fast-running lifestyle.
facts.quote: Anchiornis has hindleg proportions more like those of more primitive theropod dinosaurs than avialans, with long legs indicating a fast-running lifestyle

facts.statement: Feathers covering Anchiornis's lower legs may have slowed its running speed.
facts.quote: Long leg feathers on the lower legs may have slowed the running speed of Anchiornis

facts.statement: Anchiornis's hind wings were likely used mainly for display rather than flight, given their smaller size and symmetrical feathers.
facts.quote: The hind wings of Anchiornis were smaller and made of more curved, symmetrical feathers than those of Microraptor, suggesting that they were used mainly for display rather than flight

facts.statement: A 2018 study found gastric pellets in Anchiornis specimens, some preserved inside the bodies.
facts.quote: A 2018 study reported gastric pellets in association with Anchiornis specimens; some of the Anchiornis were even preserved with pellets still inside their bodies

facts.statement: Anchiornis is the earliest known theropod to produce gastric pellets.
facts.quote: Anchiornis is the earliest theropod known to have produced pellets

facts.statement: Anchiornis lived between 168.2 and 152.21 million years ago during the Bathonian to Kimmeridgian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Bathonian to Kimmeridgian (168.2 to 152.21 million years ago)

facts.statement: There are three recorded fossil occurrences of Anchiornis in the Paleobiology Database.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 3

facts.statement: The Paleobiology Database lists Troodontidae as the parent group for Anchiornis.
facts.quote: Parent group: Troodontidae

facts.statement: The Paleobiology Database classifies Anchiornis within the family Troodontidae.
facts.quote: Family: Troodontidae

facts.statement: Anchiornis is classified under the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Li et al. (2026) interpreted Eosinopteryx brevipenna as a junior synonym of Anchiornis huxleyi.
facts.quote: Li et al. (2026) redescribe the holotype of Eosinopteryx brevipenna and interpret this species as a junior synonym of Anchiornis huxleyi
